{{Short description|Probability distribution in measure theory}}
In [[mathematics]], two positive (or [[Signed measure|signed]] or [[Complex measure|complex]]) measures <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> defined on a [[measurable space]] <math>(\Omega, \Sigma)</math> are called '''singular''' if there exist two disjoint measurable sets <math>A, B \in \Sigma</math> whose [[Set union|union]] is <math>\Omega</math> such that <math>\mu</math> is zero on all measurable subsets of <math>B</math> while <math>\nu</math> is zero on all measurable subsets of <math>A.</math> This is denoted by <math>\mu \perp \nu.</math>

A refined form of [[Lebesgue's decomposition theorem]] decomposes a singular measure into a singular continuous measure and a [[discrete measure]].

==Examples on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>==

As a particular case, a measure defined on the [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> is called ''singular'', if it is singular with respect to the [[Lebesgue measure]] on this space. For example, the [[Dirac delta function]] is a singular measure.

'''Example.''' A [[discrete measure]].

The [[Heaviside step function]] on the [[real line]],
<math display=block>H(x) \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0; \\ 1, & x \geq 0; \end{cases}</math>
has the [[Dirac delta function|Dirac delta distribution]] <math>\delta_0</math> as its [[distributional derivative]]. This is a measure on the real line, a "[[point mass]]" at <math>0.</math> However, the [[Dirac measure]] <math>\delta_0</math> is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure <math>\lambda,</math> nor is <math>\lambda</math> absolutely continuous with respect to <math>\delta_0:</math> <math>\lambda(\{0\}) = 0</math> but <math>\delta_0(\{0\}) = 1;</math> if <math>U</math> is any non-empty [[open set]] not containing 0, then <math>\lambda(U) > 0</math> but <math>\delta_0(U) = 0.</math>

'''Example.''' A singular continuous measure.

The [[Cantor distribution]] has a [[cumulative distribution function]] that is continuous but not [[absolutely continuous]], and indeed its absolutely continuous part is zero: it is singular continuous.

'''Example.''' A singular continuous measure on <math>\R^2.</math>

The upper and lower [[Copula (probability theory)#Fréchet–Hoeffding copula bounds|Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds]] are singular distributions in two dimensions.
